definition: The programmer-visible contract of instructions, registers, data types, and addressing, separate from the circuit that implements it.
wrongs: The gate-level design of the adder and the pipeline registers.
The physical pinout of the processor package.
The operating system's file format.
why: Compilers and assembly programmers depend on the visible instructions and registers, not on the internal wiring.
example: A compiler writer chooses ADD and LW encodings from a manual and never needs the ALU's transistor schematic.
scenario: A compiler needs the registers, instruction formats, and addressing rules, but not the gate-level adder. Which description is that contract?
scenarioWhy: Registers, formats, and addressing visible to software form the instruction set architecture.

definition: The processor hardware that stores operands and performs operations on them, including the ALU, registers, and multiplexers.
wrongs: The logic that only generates control signals from the opcode.
The page table that translates virtual addresses.
The disk controller that moves blocks without the processor.
why: Operands move through registers, muxes, and the ALU, which together form the path data follows.
example: During an add, two register values pass through multiplexers into the ALU, and the sum returns to the register file.
scenario: Register values pass through multiplexers into the ALU, and the result is written back. Which CPU part moves and operates on those values?
scenarioWhy: Hardware that carries operands through the ALU and registers is the datapath.

definition: The processor block that decodes an instruction and generates the signals that steer the datapath.
wrongs: The block that adds and shifts the operand bits.
The register that holds the address of the next instruction.
The cache that holds recent data blocks.
why: The opcode must be turned into select, write-enable, and ALU-operation signals.
example: For a store, the decoder asserts the memory-write signal and chooses the register file's read ports.
scenario: An instruction must open the correct multiplexers and tell the ALU which operation to perform. Which block creates those signals?
scenarioAnswer: The instruction decoder and signal generator
scenarioWhy: Generating the signals that steer the datapath is the job of the control unit.

definition: The datapath unit that performs arithmetic and logical operations such as add, subtract, AND, and compare.
wrongs: The unit that only fetches instructions from memory.
The unit that translates virtual page numbers.
The unit that transfers blocks between a device and memory.
why: Arithmetic and logic instructions are implemented by this combinational unit inside the datapath.
example: An ADD instruction sends two register operands into a unit that outputs their sum and a zero flag.
scenario: An ADD must produce the sum of two register values. Which unit performs that operation?
scenarioWhy: Adding two operands is done by the arithmetic and logic unit.

definition: The register that holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
wrongs: The register that holds the instruction currently being decoded.
The register that holds a subroutine return address on a stack machine only.
The register that holds the ALU flags.
why: Instruction fetch uses this address, and it is then updated to the following instruction or to a branch target.
example: After a 4-byte instruction at address 200 is fetched, the next-address register becomes 204 unless a branch is taken.
scenario: After an instruction is fetched, which register normally supplies the address of the following instruction?
scenarioWhy: The address of the next instruction is kept in the program counter.

definition: The register that holds the instruction that has just been fetched so it can be decoded.
wrongs: The register that holds the address of the next instruction.
The register that holds a loaded data operand from memory.
The register that holds a cache tag.
why: The fetched bit pattern must be saved while the control unit examines the opcode and operand fields.
example: A load word arrives from instruction memory and is latched so its opcode and register fields can be read.
scenario: The bit pattern just fetched from instruction memory is held while its opcode is examined. Which register holds that pattern?
scenarioWhy: The instruction currently being decoded is held in the instruction register.

definition: A small, fast, multiported array of registers inside the processor that instructions read and write.
wrongs: The large DRAM that holds programs and data.
A cache of page-table translations.
A disk buffer outside the processor.
why: Most arithmetic instructions take operands from this array and write the result back into it in the same cycle structure.
example: A MIPS-style core has 32 registers that an ADD can read two of, and write a third, through separate ports.
scenario: An ADD reads two named registers and writes a third through separate ports in a small array inside the CPU. Name that array.
scenarioWhy: A small multiported array of programmer-visible registers is the register file.

definition: A programmer-visible register that instructions may use to hold arbitrary operands and results.
wrongs: A register reserved only for the next instruction address.
A register that holds only condition flags.
A register that holds only the current instruction bits.
why: Unlike the program counter, these registers are named by arithmetic and load instructions as operand locations.
example: A compiler keeps a loop index in one named register and a running total in another.
scenario: A compiler stores a loop index in a named register that ADD and LOAD may use freely. Which class of register is that?
scenarioWhy: A register the program uses for ordinary operands is a general-purpose register.

definition: The repeated sequence of fetching an instruction, decoding it, executing it, and writing the result.
wrongs: A pipeline bubble inserted to wait for memory.
A cache miss that refills one block.
An interrupt acknowledge sent to a device.
why: Every instruction, however implemented, is still obtained, interpreted, performed, and retired.
example: A simple CPU repeats fetch, decode, execute, and write-back once for each instruction in a counting loop.
scenario: A simple CPU repeats fetch, decode, execute, and write-back for every instruction in a loop. Name that sequence.
scenarioWhy: Repeating fetch, decode, execute, and write-back is the instruction cycle.

definition: The instruction field that specifies the operation, such as add, load, or branch.
wrongs: A constant stored inside the instruction as data.
The field that names a source register.
A comment ignored by the assembler.
why: The control unit reads this field to decide which operation and which control signals to use.
example: In an instruction word, a group of bits selects addition rather than subtraction or a load.
scenario: One field in an instruction word selects addition rather than a load. Name that field.
scenarioWhy: The field that selects the operation is the opcode.

definition: A value, or the location of a value, that an instruction reads or writes.
wrongs: The field that only names the operation.
The clock that times the pipeline.
A comment in the source listing.
why: An instruction specifies both what to do and which data to do it to.
example: An ADD reads the contents of two registers and writes their sum into a third register.
scenario: An ADD uses the contents of register 1 as a value to be added. What role does register 1 play?
scenarioAnswer: A data value used by the instruction
scenarioWhy: A value the instruction reads or writes is an operand.

definition: An addressing mode in which the operand value is encoded directly in the instruction.
wrongs: A mode in which the instruction holds the memory address of the operand.
A mode in which the instruction holds the address of a pointer to the operand.
A mode in which the operand address is the program counter plus an offset.
why: No extra memory read is required for the operand because the constant travels inside the instruction.
example: An add-immediate instruction contains the constant 12 in its bit fields and adds that constant to a register.
scenario: The constant 12 is encoded inside an add instruction and is not fetched from a data address. Name that addressing mode.
scenarioAnswer: The value is inside the instruction
scenarioWrongs: The instruction holds the operand's memory address
The instruction holds a pointer's address
The address is the program counter plus an offset
scenarioWhy: A constant encoded in the instruction is immediate addressing.

definition: An addressing mode in which the operand is already in a register named by the instruction.
wrongs: A mode in which the operand is a constant in the instruction.
A mode in which the instruction contains a memory address.
A mode that adds a displacement to the program counter.
why: The register field selects an entry in the register file, and that entry is the operand.
example: An ADD names two source registers, and both values are read from the register file with no data-memory access.
scenario: Both source values of an ADD already sit in named registers, and no data memory is read. Name that addressing mode.
scenarioAnswer: The operand is in a named register
scenarioWrongs: The operand is a constant in the instruction
The instruction contains a memory address
The address is the program counter plus an offset
scenarioWhy: Taking the operand from a register named by the instruction is register addressing.

definition: An addressing mode in which the instruction itself contains the memory address of the operand.
wrongs: A mode in which the instruction contains the address of a word that holds the operand address.
A mode in which the operand value is a constant in the instruction.
A mode that forms the address by adding a register to a displacement.
why: The address field is used as the effective address with no further addition or pointer follow.
example: A load instruction includes the address 4096, and the operand is read from memory location 4096.
scenario: A load instruction contains the address 4096, and the operand is taken from that memory location itself. Name that mode.
scenarioAnswer: The instruction holds the operand address
scenarioWrongs: The instruction holds a pointer to the address
The operand is a constant in the instruction
A register is added to a displacement
scenarioWhy: When the instruction field is the operand's memory address, the mode is direct addressing.

definition: An addressing mode in which the instruction gives a location whose contents are the address of the operand.
wrongs: A mode in which the instruction field is itself the operand address.
A mode in which the operand is a constant in the instruction.
A mode used only for branch targets relative to the program counter.
why: The processor must follow a pointer: the first location supplies the address used for the actual data access.
example: An instruction names memory cell 1000, cell 1000 contains 2500, and the operand is read from address 2500.
scenario: An instruction names cell 1000, that cell contains 2500, and the operand is read from 2500. Name that mode.
scenarioAnswer: Follow a pointer to the operand
scenarioWrongs: Use the instruction field as the operand address
Use a constant inside the instruction
Add an offset to the program counter
scenarioWhy: Using a memory word as a pointer to the operand is indirect addressing.

definition: An addressing mode in which the operand address is the sum of a register and a displacement.
wrongs: A mode in which the address is only a constant in the instruction.
A mode in which the operand is the register itself.
A mode that uses the program counter plus a branch offset only.
why: The register can walk through an array while the displacement selects the array's base or a field.
example: A load adds the contents of an index register to a constant base to reach the next array element.
scenario: A load forms the address by adding an index register to a constant displacement. Name that mode.
scenarioWrongs: Program counter plus a branch offset
scenarioWhy: Adding a register to a displacement to form the address is indexed addressing.

definition: An addressing mode in which the target address is the program counter plus a signed offset from the instruction.
wrongs: A mode that uses an absolute address stored in the instruction.
A mode that follows a pointer in memory.
A mode that encodes the operand as an immediate constant.
why: Branches and position-independent code can refer to nearby instructions without an absolute address.
example: A branch adds a signed offset to the program counter so the next fetch comes from a nearby label.
scenario: A branch adds a signed offset to the program counter to form its target. Name that addressing mode.
scenarioWrongs: An absolute address in the instruction
scenarioWhy: Forming the target as the program counter plus a signed offset is PC-relative addressing.

definition: An instruction-set style of simple, usually fixed-length instructions in which only explicit loads and stores access memory.
wrongs: An instruction-set style of complex, often variable-length instructions that can operate on memory operands.
A style that has no registers and uses only a stack.
A style that executes one very long instruction word of many operations.
why: Simple fixed encodings and a load-store model make pipelining and compiler scheduling easier.
example: Adding two memory variables requires a load, a register add, and a store, each a short fixed-length instruction.
scenario: A processor uses fixed-length instructions, and only loads and stores touch memory. Which instruction-set style is that?
scenarioWhy: Simple fixed-length load-store instructions characterize RISC.

definition: An instruction-set style of complex, often variable-length instructions that may operate directly on memory operands.
wrongs: A load-store style with simple fixed-length instructions.
A style whose only operations are single-cycle register adds.
A style with separate instruction and data buses by definition.
why: A single complex instruction can encode an operation that a load-store machine would split into several instructions.
example: One variable-length instruction reads a memory operand, adds it to a register, and writes the memory location back.
scenario: One variable-length instruction both reads a memory operand and performs arithmetic on it. Which instruction-set style is that?
scenarioWhy: Complex variable-length instructions that use memory operands characterize CISC.

definition: An encoding in which every instruction occupies the same number of bits.
wrongs: An encoding in which instructions may occupy different numbers of bytes.
A Huffman encoding of opcodes.
A Gray encoding of counters.
why: The next instruction address is a constant stride away, which simplifies fetch and decode.
example: Every instruction is 32 bits, so after a fetch at address 1000 the next sequential address is 1004.
scenario: Every instruction is 32 bits wide, so a sequential fetch always advances the address by 4 bytes. Name that length choice.
scenarioAnswer: Every instruction has the same width
scenarioWhy: A constant 32-bit size means the instruction length is fixed.

definition: An organization that overlaps the stages of several instructions, such as fetch, decode, execute, memory, and write-back.
wrongs: A design in which one instruction finishes completely before the next fetch starts.
A microprogram stored in a control ROM.
A transfer of a disk block by a device controller.
why: Different instructions occupy different stages at the same time, increasing throughput.
example: While one instruction uses the ALU, the next is being decoded and a third is being fetched.
scenario: Five instructions occupy fetch, decode, execute, memory, and write-back at the same time. Name that organization.
scenarioWrongs: One instruction finished before the next starts
A device moving a disk block
scenarioWhy: Overlapping the stages of several instructions is pipelining.

definition: A pipeline conflict in which two instructions need the same hardware resource in the same cycle.
wrongs: A conflict in which an instruction needs a result that has not been written yet.
A conflict in which the next address is unknown until a branch resolves.
A miss that requires a block to be fetched from the next memory level.
why: If there is only one memory port, instruction fetch and a data access cannot both use it in the same cycle.
example: In a pipeline with one memory, a data load in the memory stage collides with an instruction fetch in the same cycle.
scenario: A data access and an instruction fetch both need the single memory port in the same cycle. Name that conflict.
scenarioWrongs: A result is not written yet
A block is absent from the cache
scenarioWhy: Needing the same hardware resource in one cycle is a structural hazard.

definition: A pipeline dependence in which an instruction needs a value that an earlier instruction has not yet written.
wrongs: A conflict over a shared hardware resource.
A delay caused only by an unresolved branch.
A translation failure in the page table.
why: The classic read-after-write dependence makes a later instruction read a register too early.
example: An ADD writes register 1 in write-back, but the next instruction wants register 1 during its execute stage.
scenario: The next instruction reads a register that an earlier ADD has not yet written back. Name that dependence.
scenarioAnswer: A needed result is not ready
scenarioWhy: Needing a value that an earlier instruction has not written is a data hazard.

definition: A pipeline delay that occurs because the next instruction address is not known until a branch is resolved.
wrongs: A dependence on a register result that is not ready.
A collision on a single memory port.
A dirty cache line waiting to be written back.
why: The fetch stage does not know which instruction follows until the branch decision and target are known.
example: A conditional branch is in the decode stage, so the fetch stage is not yet sure which instruction to load next.
scenario: Fetch cannot choose the next instruction until a conditional branch decides taken or not taken. Name that delay.
scenarioAnswer: The next address depends on a branch
scenarioWrongs: A register result is not ready
scenarioWhy: Uncertainty about the next instruction address after a branch is a control hazard.

definition: Bypassing a result from a later pipeline stage directly to an earlier stage that needs it, without waiting for the register write.
wrongs: Freezing the pipeline until the register write completes.
Guessing whether a branch will be taken.
Writing both the cache and main memory on every store.
why: The ALU result exists in a pipeline register before write-back, so a later instruction can use that copy.
example: The sum from the execute stage is routed back to an ALU input so the next instruction adds it immediately.
scenario: An ALU result is sent straight to the next instruction's ALU input before the register file is written. Name that bypass.
scenarioAnswer: Use the result before register write
scenarioWhy: Sending a result to a dependent instruction before write-back is forwarding.

definition: A deliberate delay that freezes earlier stages and inserts a bubble until a hazard clears.
wrongs: A bypass that supplies a result before the register write.
A guess about a branch direction.
A flush that discards instructions after a taken branch.
why: When bypassing cannot supply the needed value in time, the pipeline must wait.
example: A load is followed immediately by an instruction that uses the loaded register, so one bubble is inserted.
scenario: The pipeline inserts a bubble so a value can be produced before the next instruction uses it. Name that delay.
scenarioWrongs: A bypass around the register file
Discarding instructions after a taken branch
scenarioWhy: Inserting a bubble and freezing progress until the hazard clears is a stall.

definition: A technique that guesses whether a branch will be taken, and often its target, so fetch can continue.
wrongs: A bypass of an ALU result to the next instruction.
A write policy that updates main memory only when a line is evicted.
A table that maps virtual pages to frames.
why: A correct guess keeps the pipeline full, and a wrong guess requires fetched instructions to be discarded.
example: A predictor assumes a backward branch at the end of a loop is taken and keeps fetching the loop body.
scenario: The processor guesses that a loop branch will be taken and keeps fetching the loop body. Name that technique.
scenarioWhy: Guessing a branch outcome so fetch can continue is branch prediction.

definition: The arrangement of registers, cache, main memory, and secondary storage from fastest and smallest to slower and larger.
wrongs: The five stages of an instruction pipeline.
The address, data, and control lines of one bus.
The microinstructions in a control store.
why: Faster technologies are too costly for large capacity, so recently used data is kept in the smaller faster levels.
example: A value moves from disk to DRAM, then into a cache line, and finally into a register when the CPU uses it.
scenario: Registers, cache, main memory, and disk are ordered from fastest and smallest to slower and larger. Name that arrangement.
scenarioAnswer: Faster smaller stores above slower larger ones
scenarioWhy: Ordering stores by speed and size is the memory hierarchy.

definition: A small, fast memory that holds copies of recently used blocks from a larger, slower memory.
wrongs: A disk that backs virtual pages.
The register file of programmer-visible registers.
A control ROM of microinstructions.
why: Because of locality, many accesses hit this copy and avoid the full delay of main memory.
example: A 32 KB store next to the CPU keeps the current loop's instructions and data after the first miss.
scenario: A 32 KB store beside the CPU keeps copies of recent main-memory blocks from a loop. Name that store.
scenarioAnswer: A fast copy of recent blocks
scenarioWhy: A small fast copy of recent main-memory blocks is a cache.

definition: The outcome in which the addressed block is found in the cache and can be supplied without a lower-level fetch.
wrongs: The outcome in which the block is absent and must be fetched from the next level.
A failure to find a page translation.
A write that marks a line dirty.
why: The tag comparison succeeds, so the requested word is already in a cache line.
example: The second iteration of a loop reads an address whose block is already in the cache, and no DRAM access occurs.
scenario: The CPU finds the needed block already in the cache and does not access DRAM. Name that outcome.
scenarioWrongs: The block must be fetched from below
scenarioWhy: Finding the block already in the cache is a hit.

definition: The outcome in which the addressed block is not in the cache and must be fetched from the next memory level.
wrongs: The outcome in which the block is found in the cache.
A correct branch prediction.
A register write that completes on time.
why: The tag comparison fails, so the cache allocates a line and fills it from the lower level.
example: The first reference to a new array block is absent from the cache, so a line is filled from DRAM.
scenario: The needed block is absent from the cache, so a line is filled from DRAM. Name that outcome.
scenarioAnswer: The block must be fetched from below
scenarioWrongs: A register write finished on time
scenarioWhy: Failing to find the block in the cache is a miss.

definition: The tendency of a program to use again, soon, an item that it has used recently.
wrongs: The tendency to use items stored near a recently used address.
The requirement that writes become visible in program order.
The sharing of one cache line by unrelated variables.
why: Loops and reused variables make a recent item a good choice to keep in cache or in a register.
example: A loop counter is read and written on every iteration, so the same variable is needed again immediately.
scenario: A loop counter is read again a few instructions after it was last used. Which locality is that?
scenarioWhy: Using the same item again soon is temporal locality.

definition: The tendency of a program to use items at addresses near one that it has just used.
wrongs: The tendency to reuse the exact same item again soon.
The mapping of one block to a single cache line.
The use of a write-back dirty bit.
why: Sequential code and array scans make nearby addresses likely, which is why caches move whole blocks.
example: After reading array element 1000, the program reads element 1004, which arrived in the same cache block.
scenario: After reading address 1000, the program soon reads address 1004. Which locality is that?
scenarioWrongs: One block mapped to one line
A dirty bit on a write
scenarioWhy: Using an address near a recent access is spatial locality.

definition: A cache in which each memory block maps to exactly one line, selected by index bits.
wrongs: A cache in which a block may occupy any line in a set of several ways.
A cache in which a block may occupy any line in the whole cache.
A cache that stores only virtual addresses.
why: The index picks a single candidate line, and only that line's tag is compared.
example: Two blocks that share the same index cannot both stay in the cache, because each index has only one line.
scenario: Each memory block is allowed in only one cache line, chosen by the index bits. Name that mapping.
scenarioWrongs: Any line in a multi-line set
Any line in the whole cache
scenarioWhy: Mapping each block to exactly one line is direct mapping.

definition: A cache in which each block maps to a set and may be placed in any way of that set.
wrongs: A cache in which each block maps to exactly one line.
A cache in which each block may be placed in any line of the entire cache.
A cache with no tags.
why: The index selects a set, and the tags of the ways in that set are compared in parallel.
example: A block may sit in any of four lines that share one index, and a miss replaces one of those four.
scenario: A block may occupy any of four lines that share one index. Name that mapping.
scenarioWrongs: Any line in the entire cache
scenarioWhy: Allowing a block to occupy any way of one set is set-associative mapping.

definition: A cache write policy that updates the cache and the next lower memory level on every store.
wrongs: A policy that updates only the cache and writes the lower level when the line is evicted.
A policy that writes the lower level only and never the cache.
A policy that discards all stores.
why: The lower level stays up to date, at the cost of more write traffic, often buffered by a write buffer.
example: Every store of a loop index updates the cache line and also sends the new word toward main memory.
scenario: Every store updates the cache line and main memory at the same time. Name that write policy.
scenarioWrongs: Update memory only when the line is evicted
Update memory and skip the cache
scenarioWhy: Writing both the cache and the next level on every store is write-through.

definition: A cache write policy that updates only the cache on a store and writes the line to lower memory when it is evicted if dirty.
wrongs: A policy that updates the cache and lower memory on every store.
A policy that never marks a line dirty.
A policy used only for instruction caches that reject stores.
why: A dirty bit records that the line differs from lower memory, so only modified lines are written back on replacement.
example: A store changes a cache line and sets its dirty bit, and DRAM is updated only when that line is later replaced.
scenario: A store updates only the cache line and marks it dirty, and memory is updated when the line is replaced. Name that policy.
scenarioAnswer: Update memory when a dirty line is evicted
scenarioWrongs: Update cache and memory on every store
Never record that a line changed
scenarioWhy: Delaying the memory update until a dirty line is evicted is write-back.

definition: A technique that gives each process its own virtual addresses, translated to physical memory and often backed by secondary storage.
wrongs: A small fast copy of recent physical blocks with no address translation.
Renaming of architectural registers to hide false dependences.
A device transfer that bypasses the processor.
why: Translation and paging let processes use large private address spaces and stay isolated from each other.
example: Two programs both use address 0x4000, but those virtual addresses are translated to different physical frames.
scenario: Two processes both use address 0x4000, yet those addresses map to different physical frames. Name that memory system.
scenarioAnswer: Private addresses translated to physical memory
scenarioWrongs: A cache of physical blocks with no translation
A device transfer that bypasses the CPU
scenarioWhy: Translating each process's addresses to physical frames is virtual memory.

definition: A structure that maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers and stores bits such as valid and dirty.
wrongs: A small cache of recent address translations.
The tag array of a data cache.
The register file.
why: The operating system maintains this map, and a translation walks it when a recent translation is not cached.
example: Virtual page 12 is recorded as present in physical frame 90, with a dirty bit of 0.
scenario: Virtual page 12 is recorded as residing in physical frame 90. Which structure stores that mapping?
scenarioWhy: The structure that maps virtual pages to physical frames is the page table.

definition: A small cache of recent virtual-to-physical page translations that avoids a full page-table walk.
wrongs: The full page table kept in memory.
A level-2 data cache of ordinary words.
A branch-target buffer.
why: Address translation is frequent, so recent page mappings are kept in a fast associative store.
example: A load reuses a page translated moments ago, and the frame number comes from a small on-chip translation cache.
scenario: A recent page mapping is found in a small on-chip cache, so no full page-table walk occurs. Name that cache.
scenarioWrongs: The full page table in memory
scenarioWhy: A small cache of recent page translations is a translation lookaside buffer.

definition: A control implementation that produces signals with fixed logic and state machines rather than a control memory.
wrongs: A control implementation that reads microinstructions from a control store.
A pipeline bypass network.
An interrupt controller.
why: The next-state and output logic is built from gates and flip-flops designed for that instruction set.
example: A finite-state machine of gates steps through fetch and execute and directly drives the ALU select lines.
scenario: Control signals come from a fixed state machine of gates, not from a control ROM. Name that control style.
scenarioWhy: Generating control signals with fixed logic is hardwired control.

definition: A control implementation in which each machine instruction starts a sequence of microinstructions stored in a control memory.
wrongs: A control implementation built only from fixed gates and flip-flops.
A single-cycle datapath with no control sequence.
A DMA controller on the system bus.
why: Each microinstruction is a control word, and changing the firmware can change complex instruction behavior.
example: A complex string instruction starts a routine in a control ROM, and each microinstruction asserts a set of datapath signals.
scenario: A machine instruction starts a sequence of control words stored in a control ROM. Name that control style.
scenarioAnswer: Control words from a control memory
scenarioWrongs: Fixed gates with no control memory
One cycle with no control sequence
A device controller on the bus
scenarioWhy: Stepping through microinstructions in a control memory is microprogrammed control.

definition: An implementation in which every instruction starts and finishes in one long clock cycle.
wrongs: An implementation that splits one instruction across several shorter cycles.
An implementation that overlaps many instructions in a pipeline.
An implementation that issues several instructions per cycle to multiple ALUs.
why: The clock period must fit the slowest instruction, because every instruction is allowed the same one cycle.
example: A load uses instruction fetch, register read, address add, data memory, and register write all within one long cycle.
scenario: Every instruction, including a slow load, finishes in one clock cycle whose period fits that slowest instruction. Name that implementation.
scenarioWhy: Completing every instruction in one clock cycle is a single-cycle datapath.

definition: An implementation that splits each instruction into several shorter clock cycles, with different instructions taking different numbers of cycles.
wrongs: An implementation that finishes every instruction in one long cycle.
An implementation that only overlaps five instructions in a pipeline.
An asynchronous design with no clock.
why: Functional units can be reused across cycles, and a simple instruction need not last as long as a load.
example: A store takes four shorter cycles, while a branch takes three, and the same ALU is reused in different cycles.
scenario: A store uses four short clock cycles and a branch uses three, reusing one ALU in different cycles. Name that implementation.
scenarioWrongs: One long cycle for every instruction
scenarioWhy: Splitting instructions into several shorter cycles is a multi-cycle datapath.

definition: An asynchronous signal from a device that makes the processor suspend the current program and run a handler.
wrongs: A programmed loop that repeatedly tests a device status bit.
A block transfer performed by a device controller.
A synchronous trap caused by an illegal opcode.
why: The device requests service when it is ready, so the processor need not poll continuously.
example: A disk controller asserts a line, the CPU saves its place, and a handler reads the status register.
scenario: A disk controller asserts a line that makes the CPU save its place and run a handler. Name that event.
scenarioAnswer: A device request that runs a handler
scenarioWrongs: A loop that polls a status bit
A controller moving a whole block
A trap from an illegal opcode
scenarioWhy: An external device signal that invokes a handler is an interrupt.

definition: A transfer method in which a device controller moves a block between the device and memory with little processor involvement.
wrongs: A method in which the processor executes a load or store for every word.
A method that handles one byte only after an interrupt for that byte.
A method that translates virtual pages.
why: The processor gives the controller a start address and a count, and the controller then manages the bus transfers.
example: A disk controller writes a 4 KB block into memory while the CPU continues executing unrelated instructions.
scenario: A disk controller writes a 4 KB block into memory while the CPU runs other instructions. Name that transfer method.
scenarioAnswer: The device moves the block itself
scenarioWrongs: The CPU loads or stores every word
scenarioWhy: A controller transferring a block without the CPU moving each word is direct memory access.

definition: The convention that decides which end of a multi-byte value is stored at the lowest address.
wrongs: The number of bits in an instruction opcode.
The associativity of a cache.
The depth of a pipeline.
why: Little-endian machines store the least significant byte at the lowest address, and big-endian machines store the most significant byte there.
example: The 32-bit value with least significant byte 0x78 is stored so that byte 0x78 occupies the smallest address on a little-endian machine.
scenario: On a little-endian machine, which byte of a multi-byte integer is stored at the lowest address?
scenarioWhy: Little-endian order places the least significant byte at the lowest address.

definition: A data hazard in which an instruction uses a register loaded by the immediately previous load, before that load can forward the data.
wrongs: A hazard caused only by an unresolved branch.
A hazard caused by two instructions needing one memory port.
A hazard caused by two writes to the same register with no read in between.
why: In a classic five-stage pipeline, load data becomes available at the end of the memory stage, one cycle too late for the next instruction's ALU input.
example: A load into register 1 is followed immediately by an add that reads register 1, and one bubble is required even with forwarding.
scenario: A load into a register is immediately followed by an add that reads that register. In a classic five-stage pipeline with forwarding, what is still required?
scenarioWrongs: A full pipeline flush of all stages
scenarioWhy: Forwarding cannot hide a load whose result is needed by the very next instruction, so one stall remains.

definition: An organization with separate memories and buses for instructions and for data, so both can be accessed at once.
wrongs: An organization that stores instructions and data in one memory on one bus.
A cluster of many complete computers.
A design that uses only microcode and no datapath.
why: Separate instruction and data ports remove the structural conflict between fetch and a data access.
example: A processor fetches an instruction from one memory while a load reads data from a different memory in the same cycle.
scenario: Instruction fetch uses one memory bus while a data load uses a different memory bus in the same cycle. Name that organization.
scenarioWhy: Separate memories and buses for instructions and data form a Harvard organization.

definition: The shared address, data, and control lines that connect the processor, memory, and input/output devices.
wrongs: The internal pipeline registers between CPU stages.
A single interrupt wire with no address or data lines.
The virtual-address translation path inside the memory-management unit.
why: A transaction places an address on the address lines, transfers bits on the data lines, and uses control lines for read or write.
example: A load drives a memory address on the address lines, asserts read, and receives the word on the data lines.
scenario: Address lines, data lines, and read/write controls link the CPU, memory, and devices. Name that shared pathway.
scenarioAnswer: Shared address, data, and control lines
scenarioWhy: The shared address, data, and control pathway among CPU, memory, and devices is the system bus.
